creative.body:
My colonoscopy came back clean.

Every inch of my colon, healthy, normal, no issues.

My doctor put the images down, looked at me, and said 6 words I haven't been able to stop thinking about.

"The problem was never your colon."

I had been on Wegovy for 9 months. Down 42 pounds. Knees stopped hurting. Blood pressure normal. And I had spent the last 6 of those 9 months in the worst gut pain of my life.

By month 3 I was on Miralax twice a day. By month 5 I was adding magnesium citrate at night. By month 7 the suppositories had stopped doing anything. By month 8 my husband watched me stand at the kitchen sink with a heating pad pressed against my stomach trying to wash a single plate. He said, "Karen. This is not what losing weight is supposed to feel like." I told him to stop watching me.

I went to my GI. She said, "We need to rule things out." She scheduled the scope.

The colonoscopy cost me $2,200 out of pocket. United said the prep, the anesthesia, and the facility fee were not covered at the rate they had quoted me on the phone in February. The bill came in March. I paid it on a payment plan over 4 months.

The prep was a gallon of liquid I had to drink between 4pm and 9pm the night before. It tastes the way you would imagine a gallon of salt water tastes. I had a bucket next to me on the couch. 6 hours on the toilet. I did not sleep.

The morning of the procedure my husband drove me. I signed the papers. They put me in a paper gown. They put the IV in my left hand. The anesthesiologist counted backwards from 10 and I made it to 7.

When I woke up the doctor was already at the foot of the bed. He told me everything looked clean. He told me to give a stronger laxative 6 weeks. He said the words I have not been able to stop thinking about. Then he was gone to the next patient.

The first time the 6 words came back was in the parking lot.

I sat in the passenger seat of my husband's car while he went back inside to get my discharge paperwork they had forgotten. I had the paper bracelet still on my wrist. I was still groggy enough that the dashboard had a halo around it.

I said the 6 words out loud, into the empty car.

"The problem was never your colon."

I said them again. Slower the second time. The problem. Was never. Your colon. I sat there with the heater running and I tried to figure out what was supposed to come after that sentence. The doctor had not given me anything to put after it. He had given me a laxative refill and a 6-week timeline. The sentence by itself was a door he had opened and walked away from.

My husband got back in the car with the paperwork. He said, "What are you thinking about." I said, "Nothing." He drove me home.

I want to tell you about the recovery room.

Before the parking lot, before the doctor came in, before the discharge nurse walked me to the lobby, I came up out of the propofol the way you do, in pieces. My eyes were still closed. I could hear the heart monitor. I could feel the cuff on my arm.

There was a nurse next to me. I could tell she was leaning over the bed because her voice was very close to my ear. She was reading my chart under her breath. "Wegovy. 9 months. 42 pounds. Daily Miralax. Magnesium nightly. Suppositories." Then very quietly, "Honey. I am so sorry."

I tried to open my eyes. They would not quite work yet.

She kept her voice down. She said, "I want to tell you something off the record while it is just us. The doctor is going to tell you the colon was clean. It is. He is going to send you home with a stronger laxative and tell you to give it 6 weeks. Please listen to me. Apigenin. Look it up tonight when you can keep your eyes open. The doctor will not tell you. Your colon is not the answer."

She squeezed my hand once.

Then she stepped away because the doctor was coming in. I never saw her face clearly. I do not know her name.

The second time the 6 words came back was at 9pm that night.

I was in bed with my laptop on my knees. My husband was asleep next to me. I was supposed to be resting. The doctor's discharge sheet said I should not work, drive, or make important decisions for 24 hours. I was making the most important decision of my year.

I typed apigenin into the search bar. I had never seen the word before. I read for 4 hours that first night.

I read about gastric emptying. I read about smooth muscle. I read about prokinetic compounds. I read a 2018 abstract about apigenin and gastric motility 3 times before I understood what it was telling me.

And the 6 words echoed the whole time.

The problem was never your colon.

The problem was never your colon.

The problem was never your colon.

I read for 5 nights straight. My husband would go to sleep at 10pm and I would stay up until 1 or 2am. By night 5 I had pieced it together well enough to say it back to myself in plain language.

The medication works in 2 places. Not 1.

The first place is the brain. The appetite suppression. The signal to the stomach that it is full. That is the engine of the weight loss. That is why I had lost 42 pounds. I did not want to undo that part. The drug was doing exactly what it was supposed to do up there.

The second place is the stomach. Not the colon. The stomach. The medication takes the stomach from normal to nearly frozen. Food that should leave in 4 hours sits there for 10 or 12. While it sits, bacteria ferment it. Gas builds. Pressure builds. The cramping starts. The bloating that I could see through my shirt by 4pm every afternoon was happening in my stomach. Not 6 feet downstream where the scope had been.

By night 3 I had also figured out why every laxative I had been on stopped working over time. The medical term was laxative dependency. Miralax pulls water into the colon. Magnesium pulls water into the colon. Suppositories work in the colon. Every product I had taken for 9 months acted on the same place. Downstream. The longer my body was on those products, the less it remembered how to move on its own. The protocol was not just failing to fix the problem. It was actively training my bowel to quit.

By night 4 I had found apigenin in 6 different studies. Not a laxative. Not a stimulant. A plant compound concentrated in celery juice that works on the smooth muscle of the stomach wall. It does not produce dependency. It does not force urgency. And the part that made me sit up in bed at 1am was that it does not override the medication. The brain part, the engine of the weight loss, is not touched. Apigenin works only on the stomach side effect. The drug keeps doing its job. The food just stops sitting up there fermenting.

Night 5 I found 2 more pieces. The studies that showed apigenin working best paired it with chlorophyllin to neutralize the sulfur compounds the bacteria produce in the stalled stomach. And a small targeted dose of soluble prebiotic fiber, not bulk-forming, not Metamucil, a different category entirely, to support the lower gut once the stomach was moving again. 3 ingredients working in a sequence. Apigenin upstream. Chlorophyllin in the middle. Soluble prebiotic at the bottom.

The brand that kept coming up in the GLP-1 forums was a small company called Motilli. Standardized apigenin extract from celery, not powder. Heart-shaped gummies. 2 a day. I ordered it on night 5 at 1:40am.

Here is what I had figured out by the morning the package arrived.

The colonoscopy had looked at the bottom of a 6-foot pipe. The clog was at the top. They had run a $2,200 camera through the cleanest possible plumbing and reported that the plumbing was fine. The plumbing was fine. The food upstream was fermenting. They had been flushing an empty pipe for 6 months while the actual clog sat untouched. Every doctor's office in the country running this same protocol on women on GLP-1s is doing the same thing. Treating the colon when the medication slowed the stomach. Treating downstream while upstream goes ignored. The recovery room nurse had said it in 4 sentences in the dark. The doctor had said it in 6 words and walked out of the room. The 6 words were correct. They were the only correct thing I heard that day.

The third time the 6 words came back was at my follow-up appointment 8 weeks later.

I went in for the post-colonoscopy review my GI had scheduled. I had not refilled the laxative she sent me home with. I had been on Motilli for 6 weeks. The bloating was gone. The pressure was gone. I was going on my own every morning.

She sat down across from me. She said, "How are you doing on the laxative we discussed."

I said, "I am not on it."

She said, "What did you do."

I looked at her for a second.

I said, "The problem was never my colon."

She did not say anything.

I told her about apigenin. I told her about the stomach. I told her about the upstream-downstream piece. She wrote nothing down. She nodded twice. At the end of the appointment she said, "I am glad you are feeling better." She did not ask me what I had taken. She did not ask me to bring her information. She did not ask the next woman she scoped if she was on a GLP-1.

I have thought about that for 4 weeks.

Days 1 through 4 on Motilli, nothing. Day 5, the 4pm pressure was a little less sharp. Day 7 my husband told me at dinner I looked less puffy and that my face looked normal. Day 9, on my own, no Miralax, no magnesium, no suppository. I sat on the edge of the tub afterward. Day 14 I ate a full plate of pasta and laughed at a movie and did not think about my stomach once. Week 4 I took the Miralax, the magnesium, the suppositories, and the heating pad off my counter. Week 6 my husband saw the empty counter and said, "Took you long enough."

The framed colonoscopy report is on my dresser.

My husband asked me 3 weeks ago why I keep it there. He said, "It is a strange thing to display." I said, "6 words." He said, "What do you mean." I said, "He told me 6 words I am never going to forget. The report is the proof." He waited for me to say more. I did not. I think I will tell him eventually. For now the framed report sits next to my reading lamp and I look at it every morning while I take 2 heart-shaped gummies with my coffee.

The problem was never my colon.

I am not affiliated with the company. Motilli runs a 90-day money-back guarantee. They batch-produce because apigenin degrades from light and heat, so the bottles sell out for stretches. If you have a vacation, a holiday, a wedding coming up, I would not wait until next week.

The link is below.

The problem was never your colon.

P.S. The recovery room nurse leaned over my bed and gave me a word and walked away. I never saw her face. I never got her name. I have called the surgery center twice asking who was on shift in recovery that Tuesday. They will not tell me. If she is reading this, I owe her the rest of my life. I hope she is still in that room whispering the word to the next woman.
creative.title: "Your colon is healthy. That's not where your problem is."
